title: Thy first charity (Apocalypse 2:1–7)
hook: Ephesus works hard but has left its first love

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patmos, and alpha and omega carved into the Easter candle. Your line was the first and the last.

They run their home like a well-managed company: a shared calendar, bills paid on time, kids at practice. Nothing is falling apart. It's just that neither can remember the last time they sat on the porch and simply talked, the way they did when they first met, for hours, about nothing. After the vision of chapter one, the Apocalypse turns to seven short letters for seven churches. The first goes to Ephesus, a very well-run church.
screen: `A HOME RUN LIKE A COMPANY.` → `NOTHING FALLING APART.` → `A LETTER TO EPHESUS.`

segments.voice: Ephesus was a great city, home to the temple of the goddess the Douay-Rheims calls Diana, Artemis in Greek. Paul spent years there, the Acts of the Apostles says; Christian tradition says John lived there too, and some traditions add Mary. A church with history. The letter opens with praise. I know your works, Christ says: your labor, your patience. You can't stand evil. You've tested people who called themselves apostles and found them false. You've endured for my name and haven't grown weary. Then the turn, in the Douay-Rheims: "But I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first charity." First charity: your first love. The works are all there. The love that started them has drifted away, the way a couple can keep a house running and stop really seeing each other. The remedy comes in three steps. Remember where you fell from. Repent, which the Douay-Rheims calls doing penance. And do the first works, the things you did when the love was new. Not new strategies. The first things. The warning is serious: otherwise, he says, I will move your candlestick out of its place. A church can stay busy and still go out like a lamp. But the letter ends with a promise, as every one of the seven does: to him that overcometh, I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God. The tree from the garden of Eden, closed off since Genesis, opens again at the end of the Bible.
screen: `EPHESUS: A CHURCH WITH HISTORY.` · `I KNOW THY WORKS.` · `THOU HAST LEFT THY FIRST CHARITY.` · `REMEMBER, REPENT, DO THE FIRST WORKS.` · then, large: `THE TREE OF LIFE, OPEN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Go back to a time when faith felt alive: a first Communion, a retreat, a moment in an empty church, or simply a time you felt close to God. If none comes, think of the first time anything stirred your wonder, a night sky, a piece of music, and let it come back in detail. What did you do then that you've stopped doing? If you pray, ask for that first love back.
Ephesus, the city. The first of the seven churches addressed in Apocalypse two, praised for its labor but told it had left its first love. Today's word.
Your line: the first charity. Busy is not the same as loving. That's day six hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics may return to their first love for God through retreats, renewing baptismal promises at Easter, going back to confession, or revisiting the prayers and practices that first drew them into faith.

original.note: Greek: thy first love (Apocalypse 2:4); the Douay-Rheims, following Latin caritas, says charity.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scolding for a church that stopped trying.
what it means: a busy, faithful church that kept working but lost the love that started it, told to go back to the first works.
what a scholar hears: prōtē can mean both earliest and foremost; every one of the seven letters shares a pattern: I know thy works, a call, a promise to the one who overcomes.

chat.says: What was wrong with the church in Ephesus? They sound like a model church.
options: Good works, but they'd left their first love, the love behind it all.
They were lazy and had stopped doing good works for each other.
They let false apostles teach them and never tested anyone.
chat.meaning: Christ praises their labor and patience, then says thou hast left thy first charity. The cure: remember, repent, and do the first works.

Ephesus.meaning: a great city, home of the first of the seven churches

Artemis.meaning: the Greek goddess of the great temple at Ephesus

Douay-Rheims.meaning: the old Catholic English translation of the Bible

overcometh.meaning: old English: overcomes, wins through to the end

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced 'biggest city' and 'port' claims; tied the Artemis temple and Paul's years to Acts 19–20; added 2:7 as a quoted source and the other six overcomer promises to sources so 'every one of the seven' is cited.

The promise in 2:7 is quoted without quotation marks in the voice ('to him that overcometh, I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God'), following the Douay-Rheims wording; confirm and consider adding as a quoted source.
Traditions that John lived at Ephesus (Irenaeus) and that Mary lived there with him (later tradition, e.g. the House of the Virgin Mary near Ephesus): framed as tradition. Confirm.
Paul in Ephesus 'for years': Acts 19:10 (two years) and Acts 20:31 (three years). Confirm phrasing.
'Every one of the seven letters ends with a promise to the one who overcomes': confirm the pattern (2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21).
